speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: CONDITIONS WITH RESPECT TO HOUSEHOLD
subsubtopic: HEATING-REDUCTION IN VALUE OF GASOLINE RATION COUPONS IN CERTAIN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promised to make a statement to-day on the oil situation, and I will do so now.
On May 20, as reported in Hansard, page 2845, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) I stated that no fuel oil would be available for heating in private residences during the coming winter. On the following day I amplified this statement somewhat, by indicating that every effort would be made to provide fuel oil for heating purposes in private homes where conversion to coal burning equipment was impossible. Since that time we have given very thorough study to the problem, in an effort to determine a definite line of policy, in the light of existing and prospective supplies of oil.
There are many thousand private residences now heated by oil. We find that conversion op a large scale would involve the use of materials, particularly steel, which are in very short supply. There is the further difficulty of transporting coal in sufficient quantities to ensure that the converted units will have sufficient fuel to see them through the winter. Consequently, we have had to explore ways and means of making available more supplies of fuel oil from existing and prospective supplies of crude.
There is no reasonable hope that we can augment our existing supply of crude oil. Therefore if we are to refine more fuel oil we must do so at the expense of automobile gasoline. Accordingly, refiners of crude oil have been ordered to change their refinery runs so as to make more fuel oil, and less gasoline. By doing this, we hope to build up sufficient stocks of fuel oil between now and October first to provide for household heating equipment during the winter months. It must be understood, however, that even after these

steps have been taken, no guarantee can be given that fuel oil for domestic heating equipment will be available to meet normal requirements, because it is impossible to say at this time whether sufficient tankers will be available to maintain a continuous supply of crude. If there is a decrease in the anticipated supply through a loss of tankers, we shall have to draw on these reserves of fuel oil to take care of the armed services and war and essential industries. Therefore, my advice to those who heat their houses by oil is to convert their equipment if at all possible. Those who are in a position to convert, and do not do so, run the risk of having no fuel in the coming winter.
In so far as the commercial and industrial user is concerned, it will still be necessary for all those using fuel oil for the heating of commercial and industrial buildings, including apartment houses, hotels, institutions, stores, et cetera, to give up the use of fuel oil for heating as of July 31, 1942. This also applies to all those using fuel oil for the production of steam.
As I have pointed out, the building up of reserves of fuel oil for the winter months means the refining of less automobile gasoline. Accordingly, it has been decided that in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, the value of the unit must be cut from five gallons to four. The unit will remain for the present at five gallons in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and at two gallons in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. We hope to be in a position to raise the unit to three gallons in the maritimes as of midnight June 30. The changes in the value of the unit in the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia will become effective at midnight to-morrow night.
After the ration system had been in operation for a short time the gravity of the supply situation made it necessary to re-categorize many thousands of those who were originally placed in higher than A categories. Many of these were reduced to category A. We also found that many of those originally in category A were owners of more than one car, or were using their cars almost entirely for pleasure purposes. It is obvious that these motorists should not receive as much gasoline as those who use their cars mainly in the earning of their livelihood. It has therefore been decided to establish a lower category, to be known as category A-A. The setting up of a new category takes time and I am not now in a position to state what the gasoline allowance for category A-A will be, or when it will become effective. This will be announced in due course.

Mobilization Act-Speaker's Ruling
Because there are many thousands of farmers, industrial workers and business men now in category A, the quarterly restriction of the coupon in this category will be abolished from midnight to-night. This means that the category A coupons, in any quarter, may be used at any time, regardless of the date printed on them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, June 16,. consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. SO, to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) moved an amendment to Bill No. 80. I did not deal with it at the time, and I was requested by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) to deal with it to-day rather than yesterday. I have been considering the amendment, and 1 should like now to give my ruling.
On the motion of the Prime Minister that Bill No. 80, an act to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, be now read a second time, Mr. Maclnnis moved, seconded by Mr. Noseworthy:
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that the principle of the bill before the house is inadequate and inequitable, permits the governor general in council to conscript men for overseas service without reference to parliament and is, therefore, contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada."
It will be noticed that the amendment, apart from the declaratory statement that "this bill be not now read a second time", takes the form of a resolution "that the principle of the bill before the house is inadequate and inequitable, permits the governor general in council to conscript men for overseas service without reference to parliament and is, therefore, contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada."
This question is somewhat analogous to that discussed in connection with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar on Thursday last, June 11, which I ruled out of order, as reported at pages 3281 and 3282 of Hansard. Before giving that decision I was referred to citation 775 of Beauchesne and also to citation 760, and if there had been no other feature than the principle laid down in citation 760, strengthen-

Mobilization Act-Speaker's Ruling
ed as it was by the same principle stated in May 391, I would have felt obliged to rule the amendment out of order, but as hon. members will recall there was another objection to its relevancy which admitted of no doubt that the house had already decided during this session on the same principle, and in support of that I quoted citation 304 of Beauchesne.
It is an accepted principle, both in this house and in the British House of Commons, that an amendment cannot deal with the provisions of the bill upon which it is moved, nor anticipate amendments thereto which may be moved in committee, and this amendment infringes upon that principle.
The amendment states that "the principle of the bill before the house is inadequate and inequitable". The word "inadequate" is a -general term which may in committee cover proposals in amendment of the clauses of sthe bill, but such proposals cannot be made at this stage of proceedings. The same observations will apply to the use of the word "inequitable". If amendments are contemplated by these words, they can only be moved in committee on the bill. This emphasizes the principle which I have already stated that amendments on the clauses of a bill cannot be anticipated on the second reading of a bill.
As reported in Denison's and Brand's Decisions, with respect to the British House of Commons, 1857 to 1884, we find reported at page 47 a statement by Mr. Speaker with respect to an amendment being made to the Franchise Act. I need not give the details in connection with that amendment, but in effect it dealt with certain regulations with respect to the Franchise Act. Mr. Speaker then said:
Before the hon. member moves his resolution I wish to point out to him that it exceeds the limits prescribed for such motions by the rules of the house. It is a resolution which, in reality, anticipates discussion on every clause of the bill, and on some points with respect to which notice of amendment has been already given. It seems to me to go beyond the rules laid down by the practice of this house.
That is the practice and procedure which has been followed in this house. It is, I am of opinion, a proper practice. To do otherwise would give rise to difficult and embarrassing situations. On an amendment in general terms such as this, if the house rejected the amendment and the house went into committee of the whole on the bill, the committee would be bound by the decision of the house and it would be deprived of its freedom of action in dealing with the clauses of the bill.

If the committee of the whole decided upon amendments to the bill within the terms of this amendment, the house would not be able to concur in the committee's report because the house has already decided against such amendments. The house should not approve and disapprove the same questions on the same bill in the same session.
For these reasons I rule that the amendment is out of order.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not deal with the question of the plebiscite except to repeat the statement which has already been made, that the plebiscite was not on the issue of conscription. I personally sought to make that clear in speeches I made in the course of the plebiscite campaign. At Toronto, in a speech delivered to the Canadian club on April 13, I said:
The government is not asking the people of Canada to vote "yes" or "no" on the issue of conscription itself. That is definitely not the purpose of the plebiscite. The people of Canada are not being asked whether there should or should not be conscription. That responsibility is not being placed upon their shoulders. We are asking the people to permit us to exercise that responsibility freely, in the light of the facts and the needs of the situation, according to our judgment and subject to our responsibility to parliament.
I made similar statements to the Laurier club of Winnipeg and to a mass meeting in my own constituency at Selkirk. There is therefore no mandate for the imposition of conscription for service overseas at the present time, either as a result of the vote on the plebiscite or as a result of the repeal of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Thorson
When section 3 has been repealed the government will be perfectly free, subject always to its responsibility to parliament, to take such action as it may deem necessary. The government will take such action as will in its judgment most effectively enable it to carry out its duty to parliament and to the Canadian people, namely the conduct of the war in such a manner as will result in a total war effort for Canada and the Canadian people.
In pursuance of its freedom to act in this important matter, the government has decided that it is not in the best interests of the Canadian war effort that conscription for overseas service should be imposed at the present time. I submit that this decision will bring Canada closer to its real objective than if the government were to act otherwise. In my opinion the imposition of conscription for service overseas at the present time would definitely be hurtful to the war effort. The people of Canada are much more concerned with the achievement of results than with the application of theories; and the action of the government will be governed accordingly.
When Canada entered this war, of her own free will, she pledged her national honour that she would give her maximum aid to the cause of freedom, liberty and humanity. Canada committed herself to a total war effort. What does "total war effort" involve? As I see it, total war effort means the most effective use of all the material and human resources of the nation. That is our aim, and to that end we must shape our policies. In making progress toward a total war effort we must keep in mind certain objectives, and not, under any circumstances, allow ourselves to be diverted from them.
There are three primary war objectives for Canada. May I be permitted to state them with care, not necessarily in the order of their importance, for that order may change from time to time according to the exigencies of the war. First, we must produce ships, planes, tanks, guns and other essential munitions and materials of war, equipment and supplies to the fullest extent of our productive capacity, for this is a war of machines as well as a war of men, and Canada is one of the main arsenals of the united nations. Second, we must produce as much in the way of essential food supplies as can be transported overseas, for Canada is the greatest storehouse of the united nations. Third, we must raise and equip as strong armed forces as it is possible for us to do, on land, at sea and in the air, both as to the number of their personnel and particularly as to their quality, so that they will be as effective as possible in defensive
and striking power both for the defence of Canada and to meet and help defeat the enemy wherever he may be found. It would be the height of folly to wait for an attack on Canada itself if we can keep the enemy from our shores. Both overseas and home defence forces are therefore essential. In addition to these three primary war objectives we must maintain such national services as are essential to the life of the nation and its productive capacity, for as man-power is withdrawn for the unproductive purposes of war, a heavier burden is thrown upon the manpower that remains.
If we are to make a maximum war effort we must not lose sight of any of these objectives. We must attain them concurrently, as far as that is possible to do. Each step that is taken must be carefully considered in the light of its effect on the totality of our war effort, for it is the totality of our war effort rather than any one aspect of it that counts in our country's contribution to the victory of our cause.
The Canadian war programme for the present year, ending March 31, 1943, has been set with all these war objectives in mind. It was set in the belief that it would strain our resources to the limit. The government believes that this programme can be carried into effect, and every possible effort will be made to achieve it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am making a careful statement of government policy, and I am not reading my speech, although I am paying close attention to what I have written. I shall be making reference to facts and figures which will require very close attention to what I have prepared, but I am not reading my speech in violation of the rules of the house.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Thorson
The Canadian war programme was set for the year ending March 31, 1943, with the objectives I have mentioned in mind. That programme involved the establishment of a Canadian army overseas consisting of two army corps with three infantry divisions, two armoured divisions, two tank brigades, ancillary troops, corps troops and army troops. Subsequently the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announced the authorization of the formation of two additional divisions, the 7th and 8th, primarily for the defence of our east and west coasts. The man-power requirements of our armed forces programme were stated by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) on February 10 of this year. He set the additional man-power requirements for the army at from 90,000 to
100.000	additional men up to the end of March, 1943. He set the additional man-power requirements for the navy, for the same period, at 13,000 men, and for the air force at from
70.000	to 80,000 men. When this programme has been completed the voluntary enlistments of Canadians for service anywhere in the world will amount to more than 600,000 men. In terms of the population of the United States the Canadian armed forces programme would mean the enlistment of about 7,000,000 men.
Furthermore, our war industry programme contemplates and involves heavy man-power requirements. So does the programme for essential agricultural production. I shall not deal in detail with either of these programmes, except to say that the man-power necessary for their performance cannot be withdrawn from these essential purposes of war without hurting such purposes.
It is the duty of the government to allocate man-power in accordance with the needs of the war purposes of Canada and the war objectives that I have mentioned. The totality of our war effort will not necessarily be increased merely by putting additional men in the army, if that is done at the expense of some other essential war purpose. The man-power reserve of Canada is strictly limited. It must therefore be used to the best advantage for all the purposes of war. Unfortunately, controversies have arisen over methods, and such controversies have beclouded the objectives themselves. There has been much confusion over methods. The most outstanding controversy has been with regard to the best method of raising men for service overseas. An attempt has been made to identify conscription for service overseas with total war effort. There is no necessary connection between the two. If conscription for service overseas had been imposed at any time up to the present, it

would not have made for a total war effort, but would have tended to lessen the war effort that we have achieved.
I should like to point out that while the National Resources Mobilization Act recognizes the principle of compulsion, and the repeal of section 3 will remove any restriction upon the exercise of such compulsion, the government has not adopted the policy of conscription for overseas service as the best method of raising our overseas forces. In that regard the policy of the government remains a policy of voluntary enlistment. That policy has not changed, and there will be no change so long as that method of raising our overseas forces remains adequate and effective.
I have frequently spoken on the subject of conscription for overseas service, and I have not hesitated to express my opinion that from the point of view of the effectiveness of our total war effort, the merits of conscription are outweighed by its demerits. Speaking to the Canadian club at Toronto, I said:
Thus far I have seen no need for conscription and little if any value in it.
I also said:
In this rapidly changing world no one can foretell what steps may have to be taken. It may happen that the imposition of conscription will be necessary. In any event, the government should be free to decide upon the question of conscription or no conscription in the light of its knowledge of the facts and according to its judgment of the needs of the situation as it may exist from time to time.
I have not put my objection to conscription on, the basis of necessity, but rather from the point of view of its effect upon the total war effort. In my opinion conscription for service overseas does not mean the same as total war effort. I am convinced that the imposition of conscription for service overseas at the present time would not make for progress toward a total war effort. I am further of opinion that if we do have to resort to conscription, which I hope we shall not have to do but which we will do if it is necessary, it will be only a second best method of fulfilling our armed forces programme.
After all, what is the actual place of conscription for overseas service in our whole war effort? It occupies only a limited place. Conscription could not aid our production of ships or planes or tanks or guns or essential munitions and materials of war. Indeed, by an overemphasis exclusively upon manpower for army purposes, it would lessen our success in that production. Certainly conscription for overseas service could not have

Mobilization Act-Mr. Thorson
helped our agricultural war purposes. Even for home defence purposes we felt that it was wise to adopt a policy that would not call on men if on March 23 they were wholly or mainly employed in agriculture. This was done so that our agricultural position should not deteriorate beyond its then state and in order that this country should be able to carry out its commitments for essential agricultural production.
To come to the armed forces themselves, how could conscription for service overseas help the air force? We could not conscript young men to fly and expect them to be the fliers that we have, fighting in the skies over every battle-front in the world, with no superiors anywhere in the world. No airman can be compelled to fly; he must have the will to do so. It could not be otherwise. The whole of the Royal Air Force is composed of volunteers; so is the Royal Canadian Air Force. Indeed, all services requiring special skill and initiative can best be performed by volunteers.
The situation is quite similar with regard to the navy. I am quite certain that the work of the Canadian navy, with its great devotion to duty, with the wonderful record of troopships convoyed without the loss of a single man, could not have been carried out in the same efficient manner if it had not been done by volunteers.
The only place, therefore, for conscription, if it is of any value at all, is in connection with our army. There, too, I am convinced that it would not make for as effective an army as the Canadian overseas army is at the present time.
Let us pause for a moment in order to take pride in certain facts with regard to the Canadian army overseas. The Canadian overseas army will have a larger proportion of armoured troops than any other army in the world. It will be, indeed, it is now the most highly mechanized and most mobile army of any of the British nations. Its superior in hitting strength cannot be found anywhere in the world. It has proved its valour and importance in the defence of the island fortress of freedom, Great Britain, and it will prove its power of valiant attack when the time comes. Furthermore, Canada has the largest volunteer armed force of any nation in the world. That is something of which Canada might well be proud.
It may be urged that since we have adopted conscription for service at home, we ought to adopt conscription for service abroad. However, let me point out one essential difference. Compulsory military service for the defence
of Canada has always been the law of Canada. It was not introduced as a principle for the first time by the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940. Military service for the defence of Canada is the duty of every able-bodied citizen. It is the ordinary duty of citizenship in time of peril to the homeland. That has been the law of Canada ever since the Militia Act of 1868, with its provision for a levee en masse of all male inhabitants from sixteen to sixty years of age. Indeed, that was the law also of French Canada during the period of the French regime under the militia act of 1758. It was the law of French Canada even before that under the feudal law of fiefs. Similar legislation was in effect in Upper Canada and in the maritime provinces; so that no new principle for the defence of Canada was introduced by the mobilization act.
Having indicated the limited place that conscription for overseas service occupies in our total war effort, I must also express the opinion that from the point of view of effectiveness of the army, as far as quality of personnel is concerned, there can be no comparison between the voluntary system and conscription. I submit that there can be no dispute about this. If the maximum effectiveness of our war effort is the objective of our country, as I think it ought to be, it then follows that the voluntary system ought to be continued as long as it remains an adequate and effective system. It ought not to be abandoned for a system which not only is less effective but would carry with it great danger to national unity and be definitely disruptive of our war effort.
Is it necessary to change the present system of voluntary enlistments? It is clear that it would not help the air force; it is likewise clear that it is not necessary in connection with the navy. Is there any necessity for its adoption in connection with the army? Thus far there have been no visible signs of any such necessity.
The situation is quite different from that which existed in 1917. The Military Service Act was introduced on June 11, 1917, and one of the reasons urged for the passing of that act was that there had been a falling off in the number of recruits and a very large increase in the number of casualties, and that in some months the number of casualties was larger than the number of recruits. In the year ended May 31, 1917, only 77,634 men had enlisted-an average of 6,169 men a month. In the same period of time there were over 79,000 casualties.
No situation even remotely similar to that exists at the present time. The amendment to the National Resources Mobilization Act

Mobilization Act-Mr. Thorson
was introduced on May 11, 1942. For the year ended April 30, 1942, voluntary enlistments for services overseas in all the forces, army, navy and air, amounted to 197,158, or an average of 14,763 men a month. No sign there of any collapse in the voluntary system. Furthermore, fortunately, the casualties thus far have not been very heavy. If we take only the army figures for the same period, we find enlistments totalling 112,881, or an average of 9,407 men a month. Furthermore, enlistments	for May,	1942, showed	the	highestnumber since last July. They totalled 11,918. In addition to these figures of voluntary enlistments during the same year, over 33,000 men were called for four months training and service	for the duration of the	war	in theactive	army for	Canada, and	over	13,000of the	thirty-day	trainees were	recalled for
further training and service for the duration of the war with the active army for Canada. So that after making allowance for the number of those who have enlisted voluntarily, we find that our total number of enlistments and enrolments for the year ended April 30, 1942, for all the services, is well over 240,000, and for the army alone, well over 140,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I would ask my hon.
friend not to interrupt in view of the limited time at my disposal.
May I also say that up to the present time at the end of the thirty-third month of the war, the number of voluntary enlistments in all our armed forces, exceeds the total of all voluntary enlistments in the last war, and in addition we have raised 56,000 men for home defence in the same period of time.
We believe in the system of voluntary enlistments. As the house knows, it is one of the duties of the Department of National War Services to call men for military training for four months and subsequent service in the

Canadian army in Canada for the duration of the war in accordance with requisitions coming from the Department of National Defence. Up to the present time only single men or widowers up to the age of thirty years without child or children have been called. The June call reveals that this class of men is close to full mobilization and that no very substantial number of men will be available from these age groups for any kind of military service, unless inroads are made upon the man-power requirements of war industry, or of agriculture, or of other essential national services.
The Department of National Defence has announced that 15,000 men will be required to report to training centres in the month of July. It will not be possible to raise these men and comply with that requisition without a new proclamation calling up additional men. Authority has therefore been given for the issue of such a proclamation. This afternoon I tabled a copy of the order in council providing for the issue of a new proclamation calling out single men, and widowers without child or children up to the age of thirty-five years.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, we are much closer to the total mobilization of our man-power resources than most persons in Canada imagine. Over 505,000 men have enlisted voluntarily for service overseas in our armed forces. In addition, we have raised over 56,000 men for active service in Canada for the duration of the war. Over 800,000 persons are engaged in war industry and about 1,350,000 men are engaged in agriculture.
We are approaching the time when no more single men or widowers without children will be available for service with the armed forces, whether for home defence or overseas, unless we take them from war industry or agriculture or some other essential national activities. When we reach the limits of the single men and widowers now subject to proclamation, we shall have to give consideration to calling up men of other ages, both above and below the ages now subject to proclamation. We may also have to give consideration to the calling of married men.
The supply of man-power in Canada is not unlimited. For the last year we have added approximately 20,000 men a month to our armed forces. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) stated yesterday that since the beginning of the year, war industry had been adding 28,000 persons a month to war production. This monthly deduction of persons from the production of the nation cannot continue indefinitely, for the supply of manpower is definitely limited.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Roy
When we reach the full state of complete mobilization of man-power for all the purposes of war, which will happen in the very near future, we shall then have to consider what, if any, changes may have to be made in our war programme. Should we, for example, increase our army overseas at the expense of essential war production, either of essential munitions of war or of essential food supplies? Will this make for an increase in the totality of our war effort? If it will, then the step should be taken; if it will not, the step should not be taken. Again I repeat that we must look at every step that we take from the point of view of maximum effectiveness of our war effort.
When we entered this war we did so in aid of the two great democracies, Britain and France. The indomitable spirit of Britain still lives; the spirit of France will revive. The character of the war has changed. This is a world war. This is not Britain's war alone. This is not a European war. This is a world war. This is Canada's war as well as that of the other united nations. This is the war of all free peoples and of all free nations. It is a world war for liberty for all the world.
We played an essential part in the dark days in the avoidance of collapse, but the avoidance of defeat is not enough, and Canada, as one of the united nations, must continue to make her full contribution to the cause of victory, as she has done in the past.
It is the duty of the government to keep constantly before its eyes the war objectives that I have outlined. It must not allow any portion of the war programme to be expanded at the expense of any other portion if the total war effort of the country is lessened thereby. It must face realities and not theories. It must not allow pressure on the part of anyone or any group to deflect it from the attainment of these objectives, by any controversy over any particular method, unless it is fully satisfied that such a method is the one that will most effectively bring our nation closer to a total war effort.
May I conclude with a plea for national unity and with a plea for the united effort of all Canadians and a sympathetic understanding by all Canadians of the points of view of all other Canadians. This is no time for needless controversy.
We can be proud of our Canadian war effort thus far, and though much remains to be done, we are getting closer day by day to the attainment of that total war effort to which our country pledged itself.
After this war is over, Canada should be the greatest of the smaller nations of the world. That can happen only if the cause of
freedom and liberty throughout the world is saved. In the last war Canadians responded to the call of duty and Canada held a high place among the nations of the world. I am confident that when this war is over, Canada will hold an equally high place among the nations of the world, with pride in her soldiers both at home and overseas, with pride in her sailors, with pride in her airmen, in her munitions workers and agricultural producers and in all the men and women engaged in the countless activities made necessary by the total war effort, with a feeling of duty well done, freely and voluntarily done, with only such a minimum of compulsion as may be necessary, so that Canadians may be able to hold their heads high and say to all the world: "Canada entered this war as a nation of free men and free women, of her own free will, and Canada played her full part in the struggle for freedom and liberty not only for herself but for all the world. Canada took her full share in the war for humanity."

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the 11th of June, 1917, legislation was introduced in this house for the purpose of conscripting men for military service overseas. On June 10, 1942, lacking but one day for an interval of exactly twenty-five years, a second measure purporting to establish conscription of men for military service in any theatre of war was introduced in this same house.
Whether it was the irony of fate or a measure of justice it belonged to a Liberal Prime Minister to present this compulsory legislation as if to commemorate the anniversary and to celebrate what can rightly be termed the silver jubilee of conscription.
In his speech on June 11 last, the former minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) made the following remarks:
Listening yesterday to the able and well prepared speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and also to the prepared speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Hanson), and closing my eyes I could call to memory the words and arguments presented in parliament in 1917 when Sir Robert Borden and Mr. Meighen presented legislation for conscription. There was no difference. The same arguments that I heard in 1917 have been presented in this house by the Prime Minister and by the Leader of the Opposition. No difference-no change!
And later, in the same speech, on the following page of Hansard, you have the hon. member putting the following words in the mouth of a French-Canadian Conservative candidate in the province of Quebec taking part in a by-election prior to the conscription measure:
Mobilization Act-Mr. Roy

"You see, gentlemen, in what position you are placed. You have; the guarantee of the Prime Minister of to-day. . . .
who, at that time, was Sir Robert Borden. . . . "that you are not going to have conscription from the Conservative party. Beware," said he, "lest you might have conscription from the Liberal party if you turn your back on Sir Robert Borden at the present time."
No, Mr. Speaker, there is no difference. Such utterances have been made by Liberal speakers in the 1940 election and on the occasion of the plebiscite. The same bugbear was trotted out all over the province of Quebec where the people were told that if they did not support the Liberals, conscription would be enforced by their political opponents. No, there is no difference, the same talk is being heard. The same parts are being played again. But a slight difference might perhaps be found in the fact that, this time, the actors are recruited among the supporters of the party which was opposing and criticizing those who enacted the 1917 drama. In 1917, the cabinet resigned rather than accept conscription; in 1942, a minister resigns for the same reason. In 1917, all French-Canadian members, save a few, proposed an amendment and voted against conscription. This year, the French-Canadian Liberal members, save for a small group, are preparing to vote against the measure. No, there is no difference. It was fitting that the opening speech in the celebration of the conscription jubilee should be delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I wish to quote the following excerpt from his remarks:
This demand for conscription in Canada has been made right along and continues to be made, notwithstanding the fact that, for all Canada, conscription has been the law of the land since June 21, 1940, and that, under the special powers conferred upon the governor in council by the National Resources Mobilization Act, compulsory military training, in other words "conscription", has been in operation since October, 1940, and compulsory service, for the duration of the war, since February, 1941,
That passage appears at page 3226.
I find this further statement at page 3243:
I doubt if any of us begin to realize how grave the responsibility has become of determining the disposition of the country's armed forces, as a consequence of the changed conditions resulting from the entry of Japan into the war. Immediate danger no longer threatens Canada only from the east. It threatens equally from the wrest. Let that danger assume formidable proportions, and I ask what will be said of a government, or for that matter, of a parliament, or of a press, that continues to look only across the Atlantic to one enemy against which this country has to be protected, and fails to recognize that the strategy of the combined enemy forces may well involve an attack at any moment from across the Pacific. (Mr. Roy.]
Toward the end of his speech the Prime Minister further said:
But if conscription is ever needed for Canada's sake and for Canada's future, I will not oppose its application.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker, which we must keep in mind during this debate. The Prime Minister is both for and against conscription. He sees arguments which may lead him never to enforce such a measure. The cabinet has been actively represented in this discussion by no less than five ministers, I believe, and all of them have taken the same stand. They are absolutely against conscription. They seem to say: "I would not be surprised to hear this bit of sophistry one of these days: We are against the draft and if we enforce it, it is only to spare you from having it enforced by the conscriptionists."
I return now to the magnificent speech delivered in this house by the former Minister of Public Works, whom I congratulate on his eloquence. To us, French Canadians, he has all the characteristics that set apart the French orator, the orator of French culture, which are ever to us, French Canadians, a motive of pride and satisfaction. However, I wish to review a few passages of his address. On page 3276 of Hansard, one may read:
"According to the needs of the situation we will adopt a policy-later on". That is what the Prime Minister said on February 25 last. "Later on, when the need is apparent, when the necessity is clear to everyone, in the light of the information that will be given to us by the military authorities, the government will take its stand and will come before parliament with the reasons that justify the stand taken by the government." "Later on", has become to-day.
When I am told I used the wrong expression in my letter of resignation in saying that a new policy had been adopted, I am justified, I claim, in saying that this is a new' policy.
The Prime Minister is perfectly right in saying that the hon. member used a wrong expression. He has not adopted a new policy; his attitude is marked by constant evolution. Had the hon. Minister of Public Works been in the shoes of the electors of his province, he would have known, long ago, the value of pledges made by the Liberal party, and he would also be at a loss to interpret them. He would not have been fooled by such vague statements, by promises as ambiguous as those uttered in this house and later on credited to the Prime Minister. "Later on", this expression does not apply to any definite period of time. To-day is later on with regard to the day of the plebiscite.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres added:
Yes; we have been released from pledges by those to whom the pledges had no meaning at all and no effect on the election.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Roy
However, Mr. Speaker, this condition, now realized by the hon. member could be anticipated; others have foreseen it. During the plebiscite debate, in February last, I spoke as follows at page 653:
These are the ghastly straits into which the Liberal party's opportunism has enticed the Canadian nation by promises and pledges from which it now requests a release. Before imposing conscription on Quebec, we shall grant it a plebiscite. As the government will not be released from its promises and commitments regarding conscription by Quebec, but rather by the other provinces, this, in itself, evidences the opportunism and trickery of the Liberal party.
And then, as recorded on page 654 of Hansard of February 17, 1942, I added:
It would be useless to speak against conscription and then vote for the adoption of the speech from the throne announcing the holding of a plebiscite to grant the government the freedom they wish for imposing conscription when they please. We should fear, if this threat ever becomes a reality, to be accused of complicity and hypocrisy.
That is what I then stated, and that is what the whole Canadian people thought about the holding of a plebiscite. On the one hand, those who were favouring conscription supported the plebiscite because they considered that it would enable the government to enforce conscription, and on the other hand, the province of Quebec opposed that plebiscite because it recognized also that this was the last barrier. The right hon. the Prime Minister told the house in his speech of January 26, last, that he was going to proceed by stages, and we have now reached the final stage. I was quite surprised to hear the former minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) state that he had found out too late that those vague promises meant nothing. He, along with the right hon. members, told the people they would support this measure, because they had confidence in their leader, and were Liberals. But why such an unbounded confidence in the Prime Minister? He should long since have known the meaning of promises that were always vague and indefinite.

I would ask the hon. member not to interrupt.
A little further on, the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres had this to say:
But we have never been able, even to this moment, to know definitely how many French Canadians have enlisted in English-speaking
regiments. A member of the administration of 1917, after he was out of politics, complained that even in his day, in 1917 and subsequently, he could never get information as to the number of French Canadians who had enlisted in so-called English-speaking regiments. We cannot get that information. We have never been able to get it; and when you start to compare the enlistments in other sections of Canada with the enlistments in the province of Quebec, you should be sure of your figures. We cannot get them. There are many factors that have to be taken into consideration before condemning the population of the province of Quebec or before we sustain the censure of certain military men who are mixing in politics instead of fulfilling their duties. This is a point that needs to be emphasized, and the point upon which many details should be obtained and given before condemnation is passed on the race which was the first established on the land of Canada.
Now that the former minister of Public Works has left the government, he is protesting against the unjust treatment meted out to French Canadians; there also, others have anticipated him while he was a member of the government and stood-as he himself likes to put it-as the representative of all his fellow citizens in Quebec.

speechtext: He is.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
To my knowledge, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has twice brought up the question during the last two years. Why then did the former Minister of Public Works not have this anomaly removed, why, Mr. Speaker, did he not do away with these injustices?
Further on in the course of his speech, the hon. member, discussing in a general way the conscription of men for home defence, criticized the present method of enforcing this measure. Yet at the time. Mr. Speaker, we too had opposed this legislation. I had stated that I was ready to accept the principle involved, and I also declared that it was the first step toward conscription for service in any theatre of war. This has now come to pass. The former Minister of Public Works claims to be surprised at the present trend of events. The mobilization of Canadian man-power, that alleged conscription for the defence of the country, was just so much bluff. There was less real danger, there was less need to prepare the defence of Canada in 1940 than there is to-day when the enemy is invading North American territory, invading Alaska our neighbour to the north. That there was less danger at that time, the following fact amply proves: After our youth had been drafted into the army, they were victimized in every way until they consented to join the active force and serve overseas.
Mobilization Act-Mr. Roy

The house will recall that the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) who, at present, is an officer, a lieutenant-colonel in the army, I believe, and who is stationed at a training camp, has proffered this charge in this very house. He stated, on that occasion, that all the means by which trainees were forced to enlist for overseas service were disgraceful. I quote his own words: "They are even submitted to the third degree." Forty-five per cent of them have yielded to this pressure and have enlisted as volunteers. As for the others, the 1940 act is hastily amended, in order to send them overseas also, although there is greater need for them in Canada now than in 1940. Consequently, they were not drafted for the defence of Canada.
All that was taking place while the former Minister of Public Works represented his people in the cabinet, while he was a member of the government. No excuse will hold to-day, Mr. Speaker; it is too late to complain. No one can take seriously the excuses that his tardy repentance suggest to him.
The former Minister of Public Works further states:
No wonder that we did not then get the response that I myself expected; although I may say I participated in that campaign at the risk of my own life.
However, the press is astonished that the hon. member did not state the exact nature of the risks he had to face. We know that the former Minister of Public Works was seriously ill some short time ago.

Address delivered last night, April 24, over the C.B.C. network, on the plebiscite.
Strife was stirred in the province of Quebec, in order to oust Laurier from power! How-many statements of so-called independence, selfseeking denunciations from political partisans, accusations of weakness and treason, appeals to prejudice, did we hear at the time? This national asset we hold from such men as we find in this great race, when there are no Shields to stir up passions, religious and racial prejudices, or deter them from their natural straightforwardness and common-sense through all kinds of deceptive and erroneous statements, and when there is no exploitation of prejudices by fanatics or gain by an infamous international finance which, at the moment, is standing at the keyboard of the infernal carillon whose sinister echoes blend with smoking ruins and blood-soaked battle fields.

Mr. Bourassa has certainly no need of me to defend him, but we, his juniors, wish to seek inspiration from his life of devotion, and we know that the seed he has sown will produce better results than that which the former Minister of Public Works and the Liberal party as a whole are reaping to-day. These attacks against him, whatever their source, deeply wound us, and that is why I protest. speechtext:
Notwithstanding the vote of April 27 last, the government is still bound by its previous commitments never to impose conscription. The result of the plebiscite is not conclusive, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his colleagues asserted time and time again over the stations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that it was not a matter of voting for or against conscription. What were the means employed to obtain a "yes" vote? There was a complete mobilization of the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which were placed at the service of the proponents

Mobilization Act-Mr. Lacombe
of a "yes" vote. With very few exceptions, all the newspapers of the country were in favour of the government and supported those who requested a "yes" vote. Why were we unjustly refused the use of the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Certainly it was not in the name of liberty, justice and right for which our soldiers, airmen and seamen are sacrificing their lives. It was done in order to favour party interests. All available means were used, and the population of the country was shamefully deprived of its sacred right to free and honest debate.
From personal experience I know that otherwise the result of the plebiscite would have been different from what the protagonists of the "yes" vote desired. The government is misled if it thinks that it is now freed from its solemn pledges. A small group of busybodies induced the government to hold this plebiscite to the detriment of national unity.
I know that many hon. members do not share my views concerning the best way of defending Canada, but at least they have to admit that I never hit my opponents in the back, not even on the side. I always attack from the front, as I do now by asserting that the result of the plebiscite is not at all conclusive and the government is still bound by its sacred commitments. Therefore the government should be careful not to enter upon the long road which leads to danger. It should pay no heed to the pernicious advice of those who in the name of liberty are ready to sacrifice liberty itself. Let it not trust those who, supposedly to defend democracy, would ruin and disorganize the defence of Canada. Let it repudiate as enemies of this country those overexcited persons who in their enthusiasm are determined to sacrifice our last man and our last cent in this great adventure far away from our first line of defence, which must remain here on our very shores. Let it always bear in mind that the first duty of Canadians is toward their country, whose defences must be organized before all.
There is great danger from political cancers. It is only recently that a certain man held a prominent diplomatic post. Why does Mr. Herridge refer to the province of Quebec as a cancer attached to the north American continent? Like everyone else he knows that Quebec is loyal and faithful to His Majesty the King. Our province is fulfilling its duty in connection with Canada's war effort. Thousands and thousands of its sons have enlisted voluntarily, and all victory loan campaigns have been oversubscribed. What was the first Canadian regiment to complete its
establishment for overseas service? It was Le Regiment Maisonneuve, which was raised in Quebec and made up of Quebec soldiers. There are many other compatriots in the army, the air force and the navy who answered spontaneously the call to the colours.
If ever Canada is attacked-and God forbid that it ever is-they will rush with all true Canadians to the defence of their country. They will dispute every inch of ground against the enemy. Our compatriots of English, Scotch, Irish and other extractions will then see a revival of national unity. Despite what may be said about it, national unity is not dead in Canada. It is only the defeatists and fifth columnists who claim it is. If it is necessary to defend Canadian territory, the whole population of this country will claim the supreme right of fighting the invader.
Let us examine the means employed by the government to obtain a "yes" vote. On March 24 last the Prime Minister asserted in this chamber that farmers, farmers' sons and farm hands would be exempted from compulsory military training. For many months and many years I had never ceased requesting this exemption, and on the same day I told the government how grateful and satisfied I was over the measure. I cannot express how surprised I was when I returned to my riding and became aware that the registrar was following his previous practice and calling up farmers and even the only sons of farmers whose occupation had always been farming. I could give to this house a long list of young farmers who have been called to the colours, such as the Guindons from St. Augustin, the Lauzons, the Ethiers, the Filiatreaults from Ste. Monique, the Gauthiers, the Godards from St. Eustache, the Pages from St. Hermas. The complete list would be much too long.
The reaction of the agricultural population which believed the word of the Prime Minister was quite widespread. It was even more so when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) stated subsequently that farmers and farmers' sons would be still liable to military service and compulsory training, except that they would have the privilege of asking for a postponement of training. How do you explain, Mr. Speaker, those statements, so formal and explicit, made by the Prime Minister upon such a capital question and then contradicted a few days after by his colleagues in the cabinet? From these contradictory statements part of the rural population quite naturally concluded that farmers and farmers' sons and farm hands were not exempt from compulsory military training, while others remained confident that they were.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Lacombe
As I said a while ago, if we had not been denied the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation during the campaign on the plebiscite we could have enlightened the population of the whole country upon such a far-reaching matter as the flagrant contradiction between the statements of the Prime Minister and those of his colleagues. But it does not seem that the owners of radio receiving sets, who pay the government a high fee for their licence, as well as tremendous taxes, are entitled to know the truth. The Canadian population which sacrifices its sons and its income for the war was denied the right to hear the truth. The Canadian party was refused the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and you will see on what a poor pretext, Mr. Speaker, when I read this letter which the Prime Minister wrote to me on April 13, 1942:
Office of the Prime Minister Canada
Ottawa, April 13, 1942. Liguori Lacombe, Esq., M.P.,
Ste. Scholastique,
Quebec.
Dear Mr. Lacombe:
I wish to acknowledge your letter of April the 10th regarding the use of the radio in the plebiscite campaign.
As you are, of course, aware, the government has no authority to give orders to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The policy worked out by arrangement with the corporation is set out in the statement given to the press yesterday by the Hon. W. P. Mulock which reads as follows:
"My attention has been drawn to a report in the press of to-day under the heading, 'Three Members to give addresses on Plebiscite,' and as acting Secretary of State, I wish to correct this statement immediately.
"The use of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's English and French networks, in dealing with the plebiscite, is restricted to use by the Prime Minister, members of the cabinet and the leaders of the recognized parties in the House of Commons.
"They are given free time similar to that received in election campaigns and are speaking by reason of the positions they hold and not by reason of the fact they are advocating a 'yes' or 'no' answer to the question.
"Any private members or other persons who desire to speak, provided they comply with the necessary regulations and either pay for the time themselves or have it donated to them, can, of course, speak from a local privately-owned broadcasting station."
The Prime Minister's letter continues:
The question as to whether a party is recognized from the point of view of broadcasting,
I understand, is one which is settled according to a formula worked out by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in consultation with all the political parties prior to the last general election.
Yours sincerely,
W. L. Mackenzie King.
The night before I had received the following telegram from the director of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Mr. Augustin Frigon:
Montreal, Quebec, April 11, 1942.
I am not authorized to rent stations or network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to anyone or to loan others the networks indicated to me. The instructions I have received are explicit and final. You may use private stations.
Augustin Frigon.
Where is the truth, Mr. Speaker? Is it in the Prime Minister's letter or in the telegram sent to me by Mr. Augustin Frigon, a director of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Mr. Frigon states that his instructions are formal and definite. Who gave him those instructions? One sentence in the Prime Minister's letter will provide the answer:
The question as to whether a party is recognized from the point of view of broadcasting, I understand, is one which is settled according to a formula worked out by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in consultation with all the political parties prior to the last general election.
That is nothing but a cynical joke. And so the various political parties united in violation of their solemn pledges and sacred commitments to deny the use of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's facilities to the Canadian party and its founder. Where are now these political parties which existed prior to the last general election? Where is the official opposition in this house, the so-called National government candidates in the election of the 26th of March, 1940? Where is the Social Credit party, now the New Democracy? Where is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party since the loss of its distinguished leader, the late Mr. Woodsworth? Where are the other parties?

speechtext: Where is the Canadian party?

speechtext: Yes, the Canadian party, my dear friend. I ask you, where is the Libera] party?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Right here.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
It is merged forever with the Conservative opposition, and you know it. It is merged with all the parties who advocated a "yes" answer in the plebiscite vote. Union government? Why create one? We have one right now, and it is more united than ever. The Conservative opposition, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, the Social Credit party or the New Democracy, and the government itself, said so to the Canadian people during the plebiscite campaign. Let them pull together, and in these sacred and

Mobilization Act-Mr. Lacombe
farmers' sons and farm hands before starvation sets in in our army, among our civilian population and1 in our dear country. I implore them to cease tearing away from their farms young farmers who own their lands, using brute strength to do so, as happened at Sainte Monique and Saint Augustin, in Two-Mountains, during the night of the 9th of June. Is that the exemption promised by the Prime Minister on March 24 last?
If we adopt such a measure as this we shall give to the government and the opposition a free hand to destroy at a single stroke the work of Laurier, who devoted his long and brave career to the welfare of the country, and who at the end of that career fought with the energy of a lion the conscription act introduced by Borden in 1917. If we adopt such a measure we shall be taking an active part in insulting by means of this conscription issue the memory of that great Canadian. If we reject this amendment the nine provinces of the dominion will be given an opportunity to respect once more the illustrious name of Laurier. If we reject this amendment we will save in our dear country the national unity symbolized in our local cemetery by Laurier's glorious tombstone.
Mr. Speaker, we have many good reasons to fight this bill. Would we leave the protection of our sons against conscription in the hands of the present government, which has just rejected the mandate which it received from the people of Canada on March 26, 1940? Would we commit our dearest possessions to the charge of a government that was elected upon a policy condemning formally conscription for service everywhere and at all times, and that is now ready to pass conscription? Personally I am determined to fight with all my strength this infamous measure which more than sixty thousand soldiers defending this country urge us not to adopt. In the name of more than one million, six hundred thousand Canadians from all parts of the country I am determined to fight with all my strength this pernicious amendment. Why? Because the freedom and sovereignty of this country, as expressed by the statute of Westminster, urge us to do so. Why? In order to do away once and for all with this deplorable colonial mentality which still persists in Canada. Why? In order to recall the government to the true meaning of facts, and remind it that Canada is still Canada^ that our first line of defence is here and must remain here, on our own shores. Why? In order to tell the government that we refuse to migrate to Europe with the last shred of our homeland, the last cent of our public moneys, and the last son of Canada. Why? In order to protest against this project of

raising en masse all our young men, all the inhabitants of Canada, all our natural resources, all our vital strength, unless it be for the defence of Canada. Why? Because we must, before all, organize the defence of our territory, because Canada is our country, our homeland, the only one we have, and because we are more than ever determined to defend it.
One last word. I listened with great interest to the speech delivered last week by the former Minister of Public Works and Transport (Mr. Cardin). This speech from the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres would have been more practical and more effective if it had been delivered last February, during the debate on the dominion plebiscite bill. It is most unfortunate that such a piece of eloquence is given us at a moment when all hopes seem lost. How much more precious the intervention of the hon. member would have been for our province and our country if it had occurred when the government introduced its famous plebiscite bill! One might object that too late is better than never. To this I reply: Indeed, let us save what we can still save if, however, there is still something that can be saved. But I fear it is too late unless the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres and bis followers concur in the doctrine I have always advocated-an exclusively Canadian policy.
Mr. Speaker, can we accept a condition under which hon. members who never ceased to assert their anti-conscriptionist feelings still continue to sit beside the Prime Minister who is getting ready to raise all our vital strength, all our youth, all our sons, by repealing section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, our last safeguard against conscription for overseas service? If my hon. colleagues are really against conscription, will they agree to be party to what the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres termed with such energy "the treason of the Prime Minister"? Personally, I never played upon words or upon the future of my country. He who violates his pledges, plays upon words and imperils the future of his country. The speech delivered by the former Minister of Public Works and Transport is the solemn assertion that actual events are proving that I was right. Furthermore, because the Canadian party does not proclaim the doctrine of one man, of one class or of one race in particular, but that of one nation, I invite the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres ,\nd his colleagues who share his views to join our ranks, in the next forty-eight hours, because afterwards it will be too late. Do not forget that.
Time presses. Hon. members may laugh. They will not laugh after the next general

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bradette
election if they do not join the ranks of the Canadian party; be sure of that. The interest of Canada orders you, orders them to sever the last links which still bind them to this government which the former Minister of Public Works and Transport branded so thoroughly and which will carry to the eyes of future generations the responsibility of having deceived and betrayed the Canadian people who honoured this government with a confidence never before equalled in the political history of this country.
I have the honour to move, seconded by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy):
That all the words after the word "that" in the principal motion be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that the ministers and most of the members from "Quebec" do not have a mandate allowing them to modify the National Resources Mobilization Act of 1940; that the voluntary contribution of soldiers for overseas service is satisfactory because of the dangers which are now threatening Canada and of growing difficulties arising from shortage of labour for production of food and other war necessities; that it is essential to maintain national unity; also that if there is a compulsory measure, the survey of which may be necessary, it is not conscription of men for overseas service but rather compulsory mobilization of accumulated wealth for the purpose of lightening the burden of the cost of war that lies so heavily on those in the lower income brackets of society.
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre); Mr. Speaker, this amendment is obviously out of order. If you will refer to a motion moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) on June 18, 1940, at that time it was ruled by Mr. Speaker that the motion, which was similar to the one now before the Chair, was a substantive motion which did not seek to amend the main motion. The amendment now moved by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe) does not seek to amend the main motion, and on that count alone is out of order. In the second place it mentions again the issue of the conscription of wealth, which has been twice disposed of in the judgment of this house during the present session of parliament. On that ground also it is definitely out of order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I have the honour to speak after the Canadian party has spoken, and after receiving an invitation to join that exclusive club, I do not anticipate that I shall belong to it in the near or even distant future. Anyone listening to the remarks of the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Lacombe) will realize now more than ever before how hard it is to govern this country. It is a big contract in times of peace; it is a much bigger one in time of war, times like these when every nation in the world seems to experience a certain anxiety and a certain amount of nervousness. It also shows that no matter what a government may do, no matter what a prime minister may do to try to satisfy every section of our population, geographically, racially or religiously speaking, the thing is humanly impossible.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bradette
I make that statement now because I want to ask the house to act as the Canadian people generally act in times of crisis-to be indulgent, to study fully and try to realize the situation we are facing at the present time, not only as it relates to Canada but as it relates to the whole of the civilized, world and to Christianity; to face it in a coolheaded way, so that whatever we decide here may be in the interests of the things we cherish the most. As we have seen in this house, it is absolutely impossible to bring in any policy relating to the present war which will satisfy all the parties here, including even the Liberal party itself. In his remarks the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) came out immediately for a total war effort, with which we can all agree. That is one common ground on which the people of Canada are in full accord, namely the necessity for a total war effort in order that we may achieve the victory as soon as possible for the principles we cherish. But again the hon. gentleman brought to this house the bogy that was raised during the election of 1940, the suggestion of a union or national government, something which was severely rejected by the Canadian electorate at that time. Again the hon. gentleman made that appeal; and I have never doubted his sincerity for a single moment, even when he made that appeal. He did not name any of those he intended to have in his government, but I well remember that last session the talented young member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), during the course of one of his speeches, mentioned with fervour the name of a distinguished Canadian now in the British House of Lords, Lord Bennett, a man wonderfully gifted, who was at the head of this government during one of the most difficult periods in our history, the great depression. However, that fell flat, like a frozen pancake; it was not mentioned again in the newspapers or anywhere else, though this outstanding gentleman was mentioned as a possible member of that superman cabinet.
Who were the men the leader of the opposition had in mind? I know the first one who would go from this side of the house; it would be the Prime Minister of this country. So far as I am concerned I am going to stand by him through thick and thin, because he has done a wonderful job, in connection with Canada's war effort, in maintaining national unity. In making that statement I believe I am voicing the sentiment not only of my own constituents but also of the great majority of the Canadian people. The leader of the opposition received an answer to his suggestion only a few days after he made it, 
from Mr. J. M. Macdonnell, who is a potential leader of the Conservative party in Canada. Speaking before a Conservative business men's club at Toronto on June 11, 1942, Mr. Macdonnell is reported as follows:
The party system, he said, was one of the chief institutions on which freedom depended. A national government, one which faced virtually no opposition, was an evil thing, the negation of all free institutions, and if it had to come it would have to be made as brief as possible.
That should settle the question of national government, or the so-called superman cabinet to run this country during the present period of stress. Again, to indicate how hard it is to please every section of this house, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group tried, during the course of this discussion, to sell us state socialism. By a well-worded document, well prepared and well delivered by their leader, the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) they repeated the old cliche of socialism. I do not for one moment doubt his sincerity, but I would ask some questions at this time, just to know exactly what is meant. Are they going to socialize industries only during war time, or for all time? Do they want to socialize the farms? An hon. member from western Canada asked them a few days ago if they were not going to socialize labour. One thing that has impressed me is this: They want to take -to confiscate, because that is the only proper expression-the savings of the Canadian people.
